newsitem.title: USA: NASA cancels U.S. shuttle space walks.
newsitem.headline: NASA cancels U.S. shuttle space walks.

text.p: The jammed hatch on the space shuttle Columbia confounded engineers and forced NASA to cancel the mission's two space walks, officials said on Saturday.
"EVAs (space walks) are not going to be a player for this flight," spacecraft communicator Dominic Gorie informed Columbia's crew of five.
It is the first time in the 15-year history of the shuttle programme that astronauts have encountered problems with the airlock hatch, which leads into the cargo bay.
Astronauts Tammy Jernigan and Tom Jones intended to make two space walks to practice construction of NASA's planned international space station, which is due to start next November.

"I know that I'm extremely frustrated and I'm sure that they are even more so," said Jerry Ross, an astronaut who has completed four space walks. He helped investigate the problem from mission control in Houston.
"They trained very hard ... and I know that they both were very much looking forward to having an opportunity to go outside."
Flight controllers gave the astronauts the disappointing news after waking them at 4 p.m. EST (2100 GMT) with "Break on through to the other side" by The Doors.
"We understand your desires to get out through to the other side," said Gorie.
Teams of engineers had worked day and night on the problem after the hatch refused to open on Thursday night, blocking the first of two planned space walks.

Hours of video beamed back from the shuttle and attempts to reconstruct the problem with simulators on the ground failed to determine what had caused the problem, said Randy Stone of NASA's mission operations.
The investigators suspected the problem could be with the door's latching mechanism, which is located outside the cabin, or that it had become misaligned with its frame.
"The theory did not hold up and we could not reproduce a condition that we were seeing on orbit," Stone said.
The leading candidate was a fault in the gear mechanism which drives open the latches on the door.
"We like to think that we can always solve problems and this time we've struck out so far," Ross said.
NASA managers had looked at ways of forcing the door open, but were concerned that it might not close again and prevent the space walkers from returning to the safety of the shuttle's cabin.
"We don't want to make matters any worse than they are at this point," Ross had told the astronauts Saturday morning.
Engineers will now turn their attention to devising ways of opening the hatch in the unlikely event an emergency space walk is necessary later in the flight, Stone said.

Although it has never been needed on any of the 80 shuttle missions to date, the astronauts are trained to manually close the orbiter's 60-ft (20 metres) long payload bay doors and stow its robot arm -- if they can get through the hatch.
Jernigan and Jones had planned to test various tools and an 18-ft crane need to move and install large components of the NASA-led, 13-nation international space station.

"We were very obviously looking forward to a complete and full evaluation of this hardware," said Ross, who is one of the astronauts assigned to the first space station construction missions. "It's some very important hardware for us to look forward to using in the assembly and maintenance of the space station."
NASA managers were looking to see if the space walks can be fitted into the shuttle schedule for next year, Stone said.
Columbia's 16-day science mission is due to end on Thursday with a landing at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre.
